title: Gross sales need a cancellation bridge
observed: Complete-month merchandise gross is £19,084,294.99; cancellation postings total £545,529.58 (2.86% of gross), leaving £18,538,765.41 net merchandise value.
decision: Finance should review the gross-to-net bridge monthly and reconcile exclusions against the ledger.
hypothesis: Wholesale order corrections or reversals may explain part of the cancellation value.
limitation: Cancellation posting dates do not establish the original sale or physical returns. Net merchandise value is not accounting-recognized revenue or profit.
success: Reconciliation difference in pence; cancellation-value ratio and documented exceptions.

title: Comparable periods change the growth discussion
observed: January–November net merchandise value changes from £8,406,439.65 in 2010 to £8,590,689.43 in 2011 (+2.19%). Orders change from 18,077 to 17,407.
decision: Use equal January–November windows for the management growth comparison.
hypothesis: Order mix, volume and cancellation timing may contribute.
limitation: Only two historical annual cycles; no inflation adjustment, causal attribution or full December 2011.
success: Comparable-window net value, orders and AOV, reviewed together.

title: Unidentified transactions limit CRM coverage
observed: Anonymous merchandise sales contribute £2,472,599.19, or 12.96% of gross sales, while remaining included in finance KPIs.
decision: Audit checkout/customer capture and keep an explicit unknown bucket in financial reports.
hypothesis: Guest orders or operational data capture practices may explain missing IDs.
limitation: Missingness may be non-random. Known-customer retention cannot describe anonymous buyers.
success: Share of gross sales linked to a stable customer ID; no retrospective fabricated IDs.

title: Known-customer revenue is concentrated
observed: The top 10% of 5,824 known buyers by observed gross sales generate 63.46% of known-customer gross sales.
decision: Prioritize a review of high-value account continuity and service needs.
hypothesis: The publisher notes many wholesale customers, which may create a long value tail.
limitation: Ranked over the full observed period; this is a retrospective concentration measure and not a future targeting score.
success: Revenue concentration and repeat-order continuity among approved account segments.

title: Repeat purchase has an explicit observation window
observed: 1,458 of 3,533 eligible known buyers place a second order within 90 days (41.27%); eligibility begins March 2010 and requires 90 fully observed days before December 2011.
decision: Use the mature 90-day rate as a CRM baseline; design a randomized outreach test only after obtaining consent and treatment data.
hypothesis: Ordering cadence, customer type and assortment needs may explain non-repeat purchases.
limitation: First observed purchase may not be first-ever purchase. Warmup reduces but cannot remove left censoring. Non-repeat is not contractual churn.
success: Pre-registered 90-day repeat rate, revenue/customer and cancellation guardrail in a future randomized test.

title: First-basket breadth is a useful research hypothesis
observed: Month-standardized 90-day repeat-rate difference for 6+ first-order SKUs versus 1–5 SKUs is +11.33 percentage points (19 common cohorts). Descriptive 95% interval: +6.79 to +15.88 points.
decision: Research whether basket breadth identifies different customer needs before testing recommendations or bundles.
hypothesis: Wholesale intent or existing familiarity may influence both breadth and repeat buying.
limitation: Observational association, adjusted only for calendar cohort; not evidence that increasing basket breadth causes retention.
success: Future randomized bundle experiment: repeat purchase, basket value and cancellation guardrails.

title: Dormancy contains distinct commercial cases
observed: 1,263 buyers are single-purchase dormant; 536 are established dormant (at least five orders, last purchase over 90 days before cutoff), with £1,727,506.63 historical gross purchases.
decision: Separate first-purchase onboarding research from established-account reactivation review.
hypothesis: Established buyers may pause seasonally; single purchasers may have one-time needs.
limitation: Segments are an as-of snapshot at 1 December 2011. Historical purchases are not recoverable revenue or forecast exposure.
success: Subsequent repeat rate by preassigned segment in newly collected data.

title: Geography has a dominant base market
observed: The United Kingdom contributes £16,282,882.08, or 85.32% of gross merchandise sales, across 35,440 sale invoices.
decision: Protect service quality in the base market; evaluate expansion with market-specific commercial costs.
hypothesis: Retailer location and historical distribution relationships may drive this mix.
limitation: No acquisition, delivery costs or market-size denominator; this cannot establish geographic profitability or addressable market.
success: Market gross/net value and cancellation ratio, with delivery and margin data added before investment.

title: Separate proven partition overlap from ambiguous line repeats
observed: The two sheets repeat 22,523 rows over 1–9 December 2010; an eight-field multiset check verifies equal records and multiplicities, so the later partition is authoritative. Separately, removing 11,511 repeated core lines within authoritative partitions changes net merchandise value by £52,895.50 as a sensitivity.
decision: Request source-system line identifiers and retain the current auditable baseline until duplication is confirmed.
hypothesis: Repeated identical lines could be duplicate ingestion or valid repeated invoice lines.
limitation: Partition overlap is verified and excluded from core. Remaining within-partition repeats lack a trustworthy line key; removing those is a scenario, not a verified correction.
success: Duplicate key failures on future loads; finance reconciliation under an approved policy.

title: Cancellation history is incomplete evidence
observed: 2,224 identified cancellation lines have no earlier sale with the same customer, SKU and price in the observed history, totaling £44,099.29.
decision: Investigate unmatched cancellations and obtain original-invoice references before calculating matched return rates.
hypothesis: Pre-history sales, corrections, price changes or identifier errors may explain gaps.
limitation: An earlier matching-price sale also does not prove a match; quantities and original documents are not allocated.
success: Share of cancellation value linked to a verified original invoice and approved reason.
